title: Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Section 176 (Pawnee’s right where pawnor makes default)

content.overview: Section 176 provides that if the pawnor makes default in payment of the debt, or performance, at the stipulated time of the promise, in respect of which the goods were pledged, the pawnee may bring a suit against the pawnor upon the debt or promise, and retain the goods pledged as a collateral security; or he may sell the thing pledged, on giving the pawnor reasonable notice of the sale. If the proceeds of such sale are less than the amount due in respect of the debt or promise, the pawnor is still liable to pay the balance. If the proceeds of the sale are greater than the amount so due, the pawnee shall pay over the surplus to the pawnor.
content.glance: On default, pawnee may sue and retain the goods as security, or sell after reasonable notice. Pawnor remains liable for any shortfall; surplus is payable to the pawnor.

examples.title: Sale after notice
examples.body: On default the pawnee sells after reasonable notice. Any surplus is payable to the pawnor; any shortfall remains recoverable from the pawnor under Section 176.

hypotheticals.question: Pawnor defaults. What options does the pawnee have under Section 176?
hypotheticals.analysis: He may sue on the debt/promise and retain the goods as collateral, or sell after giving reasonable notice. Shortfall remains recoverable; surplus is payable to the pawnor.
